abstract.p: Due to the rapid development of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria due to the inappropriate use and misuse of antibiotics and the ineffective performance of antibiotics against refractory biofilm-associated infections (BRI), there is an urgent need for novel alternative antimicrobials and strategies to combat bacterial infections. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have attracted considerable interest due to their potent activity against MDR pathogens and biofilm-associated infections, coupled with a substantially reduced risk of driving antimicrobial resistance—especially when employed as alternatives or adjuncts to conventional antibiotics. With the development of nanocarrier-based delivery strategies, AMP nanomaterials significantly improve the therapeutic effect of AMP by improving the hydrolytic stability, in vivo half-life, solubility, and reducing cytotoxicity and hemolysis of AMP. Distinct from previous reviews that primarily focus on AMP sequence engineering or generic nanocarrier types, this work adopts a clinically oriented framework organized by infection site—including pulmonary, bloodstream, gastrointestinal, chronic wound, and implant-associated infections. Key therapeutic outcomes reported in the literature are systematically compared, such as reductions in minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), biofilm eradication efficiency, survival benefits in sepsis models, and wound closure kinetics. Formulation design strategies, administration routes, and the rational application of nanocarriers constructed from metallic elements, biocompatible polymers, and lipid-based architectures are discussed in the context of specific infectious microenvironments. By correlating the physicochemical properties of nanocarriers—such as surface charge, degradation profile, and release kinetics—with therapeutic performance across diverse infection models, this review also addresses the current limitations of AMP-based formulations in clinical applications. Overall, this review provides insights into the advantages and disadvantages of AMP-based nanomaterials currently under development for the treatment of bacterial infections in the literature, bringing inspiration and recommendations for their future design.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: With the discovery and introduction of antibiotics, the golden age of human treatment of previously deadly infectious diseases began. As a miracle drug, antibiotics are considered one of the most advanced treatments in human history [1]. Antibiotic resistance (AMR) developed by antibiotics has become one of the top three threats to public health due to global antibiotic overuse and misuse [2]. It is estimated that by 2050, MDR bacterial infections will cause 10 million deaths annually and cause economic losses of more than $100 trillion [3]. There is an urgent need for new antimicrobials that do not induce broad-spectrum and selective AMR [4].

Antimicrobial peptides (AMP) are a novel class of alternatives, also known as host defense peptides (HDPs), defined as “naturally occurring peptide sequences (12–50 residues) consisting of cations and hydrophobic amino acids with direct antimicrobial activity”, derived primarily from the immune system and secreted by neutrophils and epithelial cells (from complexes or microorganisms as well as microorganisms) that protect the host from invading pathogenic microorganisms [5]. Not only does it remove invading bacteria and trigger microbial DNA damage during infection, it also boosts the immune response. Amphiphilic in nature, these molecules typically exhibit an α-helical conformation characterized by a pronounced positive charge and elevated isoelectric point [6, 7]. Owing to their diverse amino acid composition, variable length, and distinct secondary structures, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), also known as host defense peptides (HDPs), demonstrate a broad spectrum of antiviral, antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic activities, alongside targeted bacterial specificity [8, 9].

AMP achieves its antimicrobial effect against MDR bacteria primarily through membrane disruption, which is attributed selectivity for negatively charged microbial cell envelopes by their cationic charge relative to zwitterionic mammalian cell membranes, as well as by their hydrophobic residues to facilitate interaction with fatty acyl chains of bacterial cell membranes [10, 11]. In addition, AMP can effectively kill MDR bacteria by interfering with key cellular processes such as DNA and protein synthesis in MDR bacteria. Their mode of action exhibit potent activity against MDR and biofilm-associated bacteria with a significantly lower propensity to induce resistance compared to conventional antibiotics [11–16].

Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that certain AMPs can modulate bacterial signaling pathways critical for biofilm formation. For instance, they have been shown to inhibit the biosynthesis of guanosine tetra- and penta-phosphate (ppGpp), key alarmone molecules responsible for stress adaptation and virulence regulation in many pathogenic species. By blocking these signaling cascades, AMPs not only impede the initial attachment and maturation of biofilms but also demonstrate the ability to destabilize pre-formed biofilm structures, making them particularly valuable in combating persistent infections associated with medical devices and chronic wounds [17]. By leveraging insights into the structure-activity relationships of AMPs, researchers have engineered synthetic AMPs with robust antimicrobial activity against MDR bacteria and biofilms, thereby broadening the arsenal of antimicrobial agents [18–20]. sec.title: Acquisition pathways of antimicrobial peptides
sec.p: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are crucial natural defense molecules found across a wide range of organisms, playing key roles in host defense mechanisms. As research into AMPs progresses, the methods for obtaining these peptides have expanded to include extraction from natural sources, artificial synthesis, and modification and optimization techniques. sec.title: Natural AMPs
sec.p: AMPs are distributed among various life forms, including animals, plants, insects, fish, and marine organisms, where they serve as a defense against invading pathogens. Here are some common natural sources:

sec.title: Plant-derived AMPs
sec.p: Many plants produce antimicrobial peptides such as Thionins and Defensins, which are typically found in plant cell walls or cytoplasm, protecting plants from bacterial and fungal pathogens. Examples include Allicin from garlic and Sulfoxides from onions, both of which exhibit significant antibacterial activity.

sec.title: Insect-derived AMPs
sec.p: Insects represent a significant source of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly those that rapidly produce large quantities of AMPs upon infection. For example, melittin, an AMP produced by honeybees, is a potent antibacterial peptide capable of disrupting bacterial cell membranes, ultimately leading to cell death [21]. Additionally, the Cecropin family of AMPs, derived from the silkworm Bombyx mori, has been extensively studied. For instance, cecropin A immobilized on material surfaces via spacer groups exhibits excellent antimicrobial activity. Furthermore, the fusion of cecropin A with the endolysin LNT113 enhances the antibacterial efficacy of endolysins by increasing their membrane permeabilization capacity [22].

sec.title: Fish and other marine organism-derived AMPs
sec.p: The marine environment is complex and ever-changing, leading to the evolution of unique defense mechanisms among its inhabitants, including a variety of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). For example, Cathelicidins produced by salmon exhibit potent inhibitory effects against a wide range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. These peptides form part of the non-specific immune response in fish, contributing significantly to their survival in the challenging marine conditions by providing protection against microbial pathogens. This showcases the potential for discovering new AMPs from marine sources, which could inspire novel strategies for combating bacterial infections in various fields, including human and veterinary medicine [25].

sec.title: Chemical synthesis of specific sequence AMPs
sec.p: While natural sources provide abundant AMP resources, extracting AMPs directly from organisms can be problematic due to low yields and purity issues. Chemical synthesis offers an effective alternative, allowing for the design and preparation of AMPs with specific sequences, providing high flexibility and cost control. Solid-phase peptide synthesis is one of the most commonly used methods for preparing short to medium-length AMPs. This method involves adding amino acid monomers stepwise onto resin to yield the target peptide. It features simple operations and mild reaction conditions, making it suitable for mass production. Liquid-phase peptide synthesis is more suited for longer-chain AMPs and, though more complex, has advantages under certain circumstances. For instance, Anamika Sharma’s group synthesized an antimicrobial peptide derived from the C-terminal domains of human SPLUNC1 and calgranulin C using SPPS. To enhance the efficiency of the synthesis process, they modified the conventional Fmoc deprotection protocol by introducing a filtration step prior to Fmoc removal. This modification not only reduced solvent consumption but also improved the synthesis yield of long peptides containing hydrophobic residues—addressing a common challenge in the production of such sequences. Their work highlights how optimization of synthetic protocols can significantly improve the feasibility and scalability of AMP development [35].

sec.title: Expression of recombinant AMPs through genetic engineering
sec.p: Genetic engineering provides another avenue for AMP production. By inserting genes encoding AMPs into appropriate expression vectors and introducing them into host cells for expression, large-scale production of recombinant AMPs can be achieved. E. coli is frequently used as a prokaryotic expression system because of its rapid growth and simple cultivation requirements [36]. However, special strategies, such as fusion protein expression or signal peptide-guided secretion, must be employed to address potential toxicity of AMPs to host cells. Yeast expression systems, as eukaryotic systems, offer better support for post-translational modifications, making them particularly suitable for expressing AMPs with complex disulfide bonds. Common yeast hosts include Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Pichia pastoris [37].

sec.title: Modification and optimization
sec.p: Despite their broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, natural AMPs face challenges in practical applications, such as susceptibility to enzymatic degradation and higher toxicity towards host cells. Researchers have thus undertaken various structural modifications to enhance their performance. Altering certain amino acids within AMPs can improve stability and activity; for instance, substituting charged amino acids with non-polar ones reduces interactions with host cell membranes, lowering toxicity. Modifications to the N-terminus and C-terminus of AMPs, such as amidation or acetylation, prevent degradation by endogenous proteases, extending their half-life. Introducing unnatural amino acids like D-amino acids or β-amino acids enhances resistance to enzymatic degradation and boosts antimicrobial activity [38]. As a case in point, the research group led by Xiaowen Zhang identified a 90-amino-acid-encoding AMP hepcidin fragment from the oriental weatherfish (Misgurnus anguillicaudatus) and successfully expressed it in Pichia pastoris. Their subsequent analysis revealed that the predicted 25-amino-acid active peptide segment at the C-terminus exhibited superior antimicrobial activity, highlighting the importance of terminal domain optimization in enhancing AMP functionality [26].

While both naturally derived and artificially synthesized antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) demonstrate strong antimicrobial potential, multiple intrinsic drawbacks impede their transition into routine clinical practice [39, 40]. primary concern involves their potential to induce cellular damage, particularly hemolytic effects on erythrocytes, raising questions about their safety profile when used in systemic therapies. Furthermore, AMPs are prone to rapid breakdown by proteases within biological environments, resulting in diminished stability and a brief duration of action following administration. This limited persistence in vivo directly affects their therapeutic utility and overall efficacy [41]. Moreover, these peptides are vulnerable to environmental degradation through processes such as hydrolysis, oxidation, and photolysis—particularly during topical application [42]. To mitigate these obstacles, the scientific community has increasingly turned to advanced delivery technologies capable of improving the pharmacokinetics and functional behavior of AMPs. Among the most promising approaches are those leveraging nanoscale delivery systems. Such formulations maintain or even amplify the antimicrobial potency of AMPs while enhancing resilience against enzymatic digestion, chemical breakdown, and environmental stressors. Notably, these systems introduce added functionalities, including selective localization to microbial cells, controlled release in response to specific triggers such as pH shifts or oxidative stress markers, improved passage across mucosal layers, and minimized harmful effects on host tissues [43–46].

This article provides an overview of recent developments in nanoparticle-based delivery systems incorporating AMPs for the management of diverse bacterial infections, such as sepsis, pulmonary infections, persistent skin wounds, and gastrointestinal disorders. Special emphasis is placed on strategies targeting drug-resistant bacterial strains and biofilm-related infections. The discussion encompasses methodologies for formulation design, modes of administration, and the utilization of nanocarriers constructed from metallic elements, biocompatible polymers, and lipid-based structures. Collectively, these advancements represent a significant step toward addressing the existing hurdles in AMP-based therapeutics and expanding their clinical applicability in the era of rising antibiotic resistance.

sec.title: Antimicrobial peptide nanomaterials for the treatment of bacteria
sec.p: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) serve as ubiquitous immune effectors, bolstering host defenses against pathogenic microorganisms [47–49]. While membrane interaction has traditionally been regarded as the primary mode of action of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), a range of additional mechanisms have also been identified. These include interference with essential cellular processes such as the synthesis of proteins, DNA, and RNA, as well as direct damage to genetic components. The functional behavior of AMPs largely depends on their amino acid composition and secondary structural features [50, 51]. Based on structural classification, AMPs can be grouped into several major categories. One class comprises α-helical peptides, such as cathelicidins [52], while another includes β-sheet-containing peptides like α- or β-defensins [53, 54], A third group consists of peptides adopting β-hairpin or loop structures stabilized by disulfide bridges or cyclization of the peptide backbone, exemplified by thanatin [32]. Additionally, there are short, linear peptides that adopt extended conformations, such as indolicidin [55].

Nanoparticles (NPs) are characterized as materials or entities with dimensions on the nanoscale. While certain metals, such as silver and copper, exhibit inherent antibacterial properties in their bulk form, others manifest such activity exclusively at the nanoscale [56]. The precise mechanisms through which these nanoparticles exert their antimicrobial effects remain incompletely understood and likely involve a multifactorial process. However, current evidence suggests that three primary pathways may operate concurrently: the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) leading to oxidative stress, non-oxidative interactions such as membrane disruption or physical damage, and the secondary binding of released metal ions to cellular components—including proteins and nucleic acids—interfering with essential biological functions.These combined actions make metal-based nanoparticles promising candidates for use in antimicrobial applications, particularly in combination with other therapeutic agents like antimicrobial peptides [57]. The integration of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) with nanotechnology has led to the development of innovative therapeutic strategies. These nano-formulated AMPs not only retain or even enhance antibacterial potency but also demonstrate increased resistance to degradation by proteases, hydrolytic agents, oxidative stress, and light exposure. Additionally, these nano-platforms enable multifaceted functionalities, including precise bacterial targeting, stimuli-responsive behavior (e.g., triggered by pH or reactive oxygen species), improved mucosal penetration, and diminished toxicity [58, 59].

Recent developments in nanoscale technologies have significantly enhanced the therapeutic potential of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) across a wide range of infectious disease models [60]. These include systemic infections such as sepsis [43], respiratory tract infections [61], persistent skin wound infections [62], gastrointestinal-related bacterial diseases [63], and other bacterial infections [64, 65]. In particular, polymer-based nanocarriers have been increasingly utilized in the treatment of sepsis and lung infections due to their favorable biocompatibility, controlled biodegradation rates, and efficient payload capacity. By encapsulating AMPs within these matrices, researchers have successfully reduced cytotoxic effects, including hemolysis, while also protecting the peptides from proteolytic degradation in biological environments.One notable advantage of polymer-based delivery systems is their ability to facilitate AMP transport across physiological barriers, such as the pulmonary epithelium and the blood-brain barrier. However, the synthesis of synthetic polymeric nanoparticles often involves the use of organic solvents, which may compromise the structural integrity and bioactivity of the loaded AMPs. Moreover, drug loading efficiency in hydrophobic polymeric formulations remains relatively low—typically less than 10%—posing a major challenge for their practical application as effective delivery platforms.

In the context of chronic wound management, various nanostructured materials—including inorganic nanoparticles, lipid-based vesicles, and biodegradable polymers—have been combined with AMPs to improve localized antimicrobial activity. Embedding AMPs directly into biodegradable polymer dressings in the form of hydrogels or nanofibrous scaffolds has emerged as a promising approach for treating non-healing wounds. Such systems not only preserve the antibacterial properties of AMPs but also support tissue regeneration by maintaining a moist wound environment conducive to healing. Nevertheless, careful modification of the carrier matrix is necessary to optimize peptide-polymer interactions and prevent premature release of the active agent.For gastrointestinal infections, AMP-loaded nanomaterials based on both inorganic and polymeric frameworks have demonstrated improved specificity toward pathogenic bacteria, minimizing collateral damage to the host’s commensal microbiota. Despite these benefits, long-term safety assessments regarding the accumulation and toxicity of these nanocarriers remain limited and require further investigation. Importantly, some AMPs possess intrinsic amphiphilic properties that allow them to self-assemble into nanoparticle-like structures without the need for additional excipients. This unique behavior enables sustained antimicrobial activity while reducing off-target side effects. However, current studies evaluating the efficacy of novel AMP-based nanoformulations against multidrug-resistant pathogens and microbial biofilms remain sparse, highlighting a significant gap between preclinical research and clinical translation.

sec.title: Drug delivery
sec.p: Among the various inorganic nanoparticle-based delivery systems explored for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) applications, gold nanoparticles (Au NPs) and silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) represent two of the most extensively studied platforms [66]. In particular, Au NPs have garnered significant attention as effective carriers for therapeutic agents due to their favorable biocompatibility, low cytotoxicity, and minimal immunogenic response within biological systems [29, 67, 68].These properties make them especially suitable for targeted delivery in diverse medical fields, including cancer therapy, vaccine development, and antimicrobial treatment. Additionally, Au NPs demonstrate the ability to facilitate drug penetration across biological barriers at infection sites, thereby enhancing localized therapeutic effects. One of the key advantages of Au NPs lies in their tunable size and morphology, which allows for precise control over particle characteristics. This feature enables a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, making them highly efficient platforms for conjugating AMPs at elevated densities [69]. The increased loading capacity not only enhances antimicrobial efficacy but also improves the stability and controlled release of peptides in physiological environments. Compared to Au NPs, Ag NPs are more commonly associated with intrinsic antimicrobial activity, which can be further enhanced when combined with AMPs; however, their potential toxicity remains a concern that requires careful modulation through surface functionalization or dosage optimization.

The hydrophilic cationic host defense peptide LL37 (LLGDFFRKSKEKIGKEFKRIVQRIKDFLRNLVPRTESC) is an essential component of the innate immune system, forming the first line of defense against pathogens [70]. LL37, predominantly present in human skin, drives angiogenesis and epithelial regeneration, key processes contributing to tissue regeneration [71]. Beyond its broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, LL37 is frequently combined with gold nanoparticle (Au NP) vectors for treating wound infections. Comune et al. developed LL37-conjugated Au NPs (~ 21 nm), where the peptide is fixed to the Au NP shell [72]. These constructs enhanced keratinocyte migration and upregulated IL-6, collagen, and VEGF expression. In a murine acute wound model, LL37-Au NP treatment achieved complete healing within 10 days, significantly outperforming free LL37 peptide (70% healing at day 10; Fig. 1A), while demonstrating good biosafety and eventual skin clearance. Similarly, Wang et al. designed AuNP@LL37 via thiol ligand exchange (LL37 MW: 5178 Da) for diabetic wound management. Further complexation with pro-angiogenic VEGF plasmids (AuNP@LL37/pDNA) substantially improved keratinocyte transfection efficiency at low concentrations (15 µg/mL) [43]. This complex exhibited cellular entry, nuclear targeting, and potent activity (99% inhibition) against clinical diabetic wound MRSA isolates. In diabetic murine MRSA-infected wounds, AuNP@LL37/pDNA accelerated angiogenesis and healing through VEGF expression, showing bactericidal efficacy comparable to vancomycin without organ toxicity. Complementing these studies, Ferreira et al. characterized the LL37-SH/Au NP interaction thermodynamically. Free energy surface analysis revealed cysteine residues promote faster adsorption and lower conformational entropy than unmodified LL37. LL37-SH/Au NPs displayed increased solvent accessibility and functional group distance from the peptide backbone, suggesting enhanced bioactivity stems from peptide elongation and optimized functional group presentation upon Au NP binding [73].

Building on silver’s historical use as an antibacterial agent [74], nanotechnology has propelled silver nanoparticles (Ag NPs) to the forefront, particularly as carriers for antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) alongside gold NPs [75]. Ye et al. developed synergistic Dpep-Ag nanoclusters (NCs; 1.25 nm) by capping Ag NCs with the AMP Dpep (CCLLLLRRRRR) during a reduction-decomposition-reduction synthesis [33]. The cationic Dpep enables two key actions: (1) electrostatic attraction to Gram-negative bacteria (e.g., E. coli) for cellular uptake, and (2) specific targeting of surface lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to enhance membrane penetration. Consequently, Dpep-Ag NCs showed a ~ 100-fold lower MIC against Gram-negative bacteria than commercial 30-nm Ag NPs. In an infected rat wound model (0.25 cm²), Dpep-Ag NC treatment yielded 91% healing at day 5, outperforming the Opep-Ag NC control (80%) and confirming enhanced healing rates. The superior activity of Dpep-Ag NCs over other NCs (e.g., BSA-Ag NCs) is attributed to Dpep’s potent LPS targeting and elevated positive charge derived from its capping role (Fig. 1B).

sec.title: Biomedical wound dressing
sec.p: Biomedical dressing materials offer advantages like excellent biocompatibility, low toxicity, sustained drug release, and tunable pharmacokinetics, making them ideal carriers for bioactive wound dressings (e.g., membranes, hydrogels, foams, nanofibers) [76, 77]. Hydrogels—3D hydrous networks of synthetic/natural polymers—provide a protective microenvironment that preserves peptide structure/activity while reducing enzymatic degradation. Recent advances leverage hydrogel properties (polymer density, charge, mesh size, crosslinking density) to engineer antimicrobial delivery vectors with controlled encapsulation and release [78]. To enhance localized wound therapy, Luo et al. developed a Pluronic F-127 hydrogel loaded with HD5-derived nanodefensin (NDEF gel; Fig. 2A and B) [79]. Compared to HD5, ampicillin, and kanamycin, ND exhibited superior in vitro bactericidal activity against MRSA and significantly stimulated fibroblast migration/myofibroblast differentiation. In a rat excisional wound model, NDEF gel accelerated wound closure after 4 days vs. ND solution or Prontosan® (clinical hydrogel), concurrently reducing bacterial load (Fig. 2C and D). Histological analysis revealed elevated collagen deposition, cytokeratin 14 expression, vascular endothelial cell enrichment, and diminished macrophage infiltration—indicating NDEF gel promotes angiogenesis, re-epithelialization, and inflammation resolution.

To protect the hBD-3 fragment (D1-23) from degradation and enable controlled release on tooth surfaces, Aida et al. developed a liquid crystal system (LCS) comprising polycarbonate 971P, polycarbonate 974P, polyoxyethylene-(5)-cetyl alcohol, and oleic acid [80]. When hydrated with artificial saliva, the D1-23-loaded LCS demonstrated superior antibacterial efficacy against S. mutans compared to free peptide, highlighting its potential for safe caries prevention and treatment.

Beyond natural biodegradable polymers (e.g., polylactic acid, proteins), nucleic acids like DNA serve as versatile hydrogel carriers for AMP delivery due to sequence programmability, low toxicity, and molecular recognition capabilities [81]. In Obuobi et al.’s study [82], cationic AMP L12 ((LKKL)₃) was loaded into a polyanionic Y-shaped DNA nanostructure hydrogel. Monomeric units were crosslinked via complementary sequences on L-shaped connectors, forming a network to treat Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29,737-infected wounds. Applying L12-DNA hydrogel (0.5% w/v) ex vivo to porcine skin explants reduced bacterial burden by > 99% within 24 h versus untreated controls. In S. aureus-infected murine excision wounds, the hydrogel accelerated closure after 10 days versus controls, confirming enhanced healing. This platform further enabled antimicrobial material design (e.g., functionalized sutures). However, improving DNA hydrogel stability in physiological environments remains a critical challenge.

Biodegradable polymer nanocapsules enhance antimicrobial peptide (AMP) delivery by preserving antibacterial activity, improving in vivo stability, and reducing systemic toxicity—making them ideal AMP carriers. Beyond nanocapsules, diverse strategies (hydrogels, membranes, nanofibers, foams) enable direct AMP encapsulation within bioactive wound dressings. Among these, hydrogels represent a promising platform, offering controlled AMP release while maintaining essential wound hydration. However, weak hydrogel-AMP interactions often cause initial burst release, which risks toxicity from excessive peptide exposure and compromises long-term antibacterial efficacy. To address this, nanoparticle (NP) or microchip integration has been explored for enhanced release control. Future AMP formulations for wound infection therapy must meet key criteria: (1) Biocompatibility & biodegradability of all components; (2) Minimal toxicity with immunomodulatory potential; (3) Multifunctional activity supporting infection control, epithelial regeneration, and granulation tissue formation to accelerate healing.

sec.title: Bacterial lung infection
sec.p: Lung infections frequently involve Gram-negative pathogens like Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, along with Gram-positive bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus. These pathogens drive chronic inflammatory lung diseases including cystic fibrosis (CF), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and ventilator-associated pneumonia [83]. Notably, Pseudomonas aeruginosa–a Gram-negative facultative aerobe–employs virulence factors to evade immune responses, forms antibiotic-resistant biofilms, and is a predominant cause of these infections [84, 85]. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent promising therapeutic candidates due to their dual functionality: potent antibacterial activity and wound-healing promotion through airway epithelial repair and angiogenesis stimulation. However, pulmonary delivery barriers–mucus entrapment and epithelial impermeability – limit direct AMP administration. Developing strategies to transport AMPs across these biological barriers into conductive airways is therefore critical for treating lung infections [86].

Colistin (Col), a cationic antimicrobial peptide (AMP), clinically treats Gram-negative infections by binding anionic LPS in the outer membrane, disrupting membrane integrity and causing cell death [87]. However, its nephrotoxicity and sequestration by anionic proteins/polyaspartic acid in the pulmonary extracellular matrix severely limit lung bioavailability. In Transwell® assays, chitosan (CS)-modified nanoparticles demonstrated superior artificial mucus penetration versus polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-modified NPs (70% vs. 40% within 6 h; Fig. 3A, B). Despite this advantage, CS-NPs showed negligible anti-biofilm activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa over 72 h. In contrast, PVA-NPs achieved 50% eradication of established biofilms and inhibited new biofilm formation for 72 h. While this study informs rational design of nano-engineered pulmonary antibiotics, the absence of in vivo anti-biofilm efficacy data against P. aeruginosa precludes advocating further development of this specific system.

sec.p: Beyond Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus is a prevalent pathogen in pulmonary infections. Conventional antibiotic treatment often fails due to S. aureus’s ability to invade airway epithelial cells, where intracellular persistence limits antibiotic bioavailability and causes recurrent infections. Nanodelivery systems offer a promising solution for targeted antimicrobial delivery to infected host cells [88]. Plectasin (sequence: GFGCNGPWDEDDMQCHNHCKSIKGYKGGYCAKGGFVCK CY; MW: 4.4 kDa), a cationic fungal defense peptide, exhibits potent gram-positive bactericidal activity by binding lipid II – a key bacterial cell wall precursor [31, 89]. Waters et al. engineered plectasin-loaded PLGA nanoparticles (mean diameter: 200 nm; EE: 71.0 ± 0.3–90.6 ± 1.7%; LC: 0.57 ± 0.01–1.77 ± 0.01%) that enhance cellular uptake in human lung epithelial cells and macrophages. Crucially, nanoencapsulation reduced plectasin’s half-maximal effective concentration (EC₅₀) to 0.80 µg/mL – demonstrating significantly enhanced potency [90].

Weide et al. compared two nanocarriers for delivering hydrophilic AMP A139: glucan-based single-chain polymer nanoparticles (PNPs, ~ 20 nm) and self-assembled micellar colloidal lipids (MCLs, ~ 15 nm), both achieving 100% encapsulation efficiency [34]. Nanoformulation markedly diminishes the cytotoxicity and hemolytic activity of A139 while enhancing its bioavailability and pulmonary retention. Structurally derived from Arenicola marina’s arenicin-3, A139 exerts bactericidal effects by inducing membrane permeability and ATP release. It exhibits potent activity against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens with minimal host cell toxicity [91]. Aa-139 is connected to PNPs by electrostatic interaction or enclosed in the hydrophobic nucleus of MCL. Free AA 139 enabled K. neumoniae to almost completely eliminate K within 2 h at 4 mg·L-1 concentration. In vitro antibacterial experiments, the bactericidal activity of A139-PNPS and A139-MCL against K. pneumoniae after 24 h at 8 mg·mL-1 was similar to that of free A139. In K. in a rat model of pneumonia-induced pneumonia sepsis, treatment with 0.25 mg free A139 per rat showed no improvement in survival, and treatment with 0.25 mg and 0.5 mg Administration of A139-PNPs at 0.25 mg and 0.5 mg per rat significantly prolonged survival in infected rats, extending lifespans to 9 and 11 days, respectively. Similarly, A139-MCL at doses of 0.25 mg and 0.5 mg extended survival beyond 11 days in infected rats.

A review of the existing literature indicates that research on the pulmonary delivery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) using nanocarriers remains limited. Among the available systems, inhalation therapy has emerged as the primary route of administration for drug-loaded nanomaterials due to its advantages of a short delivery pathway and rapid onset of action [92–95]. However, it is important to note that operational errors in commonly used clinical nebulization devices (jet/ultrasonic nebulizers) may cause local drug concentrations to deviate from the therapeutic window, a technical bottleneck that requires further investigation. Notably, AMP delivery systems assisted by nanoparticle technology have demonstrated significant synergistic effects in the treatment of pulmonary infections, potentially offering a revolutionary alternative to traditional antibiotic therapies.

sec.title: Gastrointestinal infection
sec.p: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), a spiral-shaped Gram-negative bacterium, has colonized the gastric mucosa of nearly half the world’s population and is recognized as a major etiological factor in the development of chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric adenocarcinoma [99, 100]. While the standard triple therapy regimen (proton pump inhibitor combined with two antibiotics) can eradicate H. pylori, its non-selective bactericidal action disrupts the intestinal microbiota balance—a microbiota involved in various physiological processes and immune regulation [101, 102]. Additionally, the rise in bacterial resistance significantly reduces the efficacy of triple therapy.Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) target H. pylori by disrupting bacterial membrane structures, but their proteolytic instability in the stomach severely limits their antimicrobial efficacy in vivo [103, 104]. To solve this problem, Zhang et al. prepared pexiganan nanoparticles (PNP) composed of chitosan-alginate gel by ionic gelation, with a particle size of 415 ± 26 nm, Zeta potential of 47.78 ± 3.5 mV, and EE of 82.8% ± 4.5%. Pexiganan (GIGKFLK KAKKFGKAFVKILKK) is a synthetic analogue of the natural peptide mag pexiganin from the skin of the African clawed frog, whose broad antibacterial profile has been commonly studied, including against H. Helicobacter pylori. In a rat model of H. pylori infection, chitosan-alginate nanoparticles (PNP) demonstrated superior efficacy over free pexiganan:1 mg/kg PNP achieved greater bacterial eradication than 10 mg/kg free pexiganan; 10 mg/kg PNP achieved complete eradication (100%) of H. pylori; 30 mg/kg free pexiganan failed to eliminate H. pylori completely. The chitosan-sodium alginate nano-sustained-release system adheres to negatively charged gastric mucosa through non-covalent interactions (electrostatic forces, polyvalent adhesion, van der Waals forces, and hydrogen bonding). This dual-function mechanism:1. Protects acid-sensitive drugs from degradation; 2. Enhances transmucosal drug penetration. In addition, in order to improve AMP against H.pylori, Parreira et al. added aminocaproic acid (ahx) spacer and additional CYS to replace one amino acid (pexiganan) of MSI-78 to synthesize MSI-78 A (GIGKFLKKAKFAKAFVKILKK) [105]. It was further covalently grafted onto biotin and tetraethylene glycol (EG 4) -terminated mercaptan self-assembled monomolecular membrane (biotin-SAM) and maleimide-terminated polyethylene glycol septon (EG 11-MAL) chemically linked to AMP by mercaptan - maleimide. The surface of ethylene glycol seal can effectively adsorb H. pylori cells are provided against H. pylori. In addition, the covalent connection between EG 11-MAL and CYS can enhance AMP exposure and thus improve H resistance. The antibacterial evaluation of MSI 78 A (30.3 ± 1.2 ng·cm− 2) showed that 98% of H.pylori was eradicated within 2 h.

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) demonstrate broad therapeutic potential beyond H. pylori eradication, effectively combatting gastrointestinal pathogens including E. coli, Salmonella Typhimurium (STM), and Listeria monocytogenes. Notably, human α-defensin 5 (HD5) shows efficacy against both systemic infections (e.g., sepsis, chronic wounds) and GI infections [30, 106, 107]. Zhao et al. engineered an enzyme-resistant HD5 mutant (T7E21R-HD5) through C-terminal arginine substitutions and encapsulated it in mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) [108]. Specifically, non-toxic NP (MSN@T7 E21 R-HD 5@SCN) has 70% EE, which consists of an MSN core (which can carry peptides to penetrate the outer and inner membranes of bacteria) and a laciatised casein (SCN) shell (a milk protein that is stable in the stomach but can be specifically degraded by intestinal proteases). Avoid the release of T7 E21 R-HD 5 from MSN in the stomach and promote intestinal delivery. Studies on the antibacterial effects of nanoparticles in vivo have shown that the number of multidrug-resistant E. coli that are orally administered with nanoparticles is significantly reduced. Within 12 hours after treatment with T7 E21 R-HD 5, MSN@T7 E21 R-HD 5, and MSN@T7 E21 R-HD 5@SCN, 60 mg/kg doses of MDR E. coli (2.5 × 108 CFU, ig) were reduced in mice. Bacteria in MDR E. coli (2.5 × 108 CFU, ig) decreased within 12 hours after treatment with MDR E. coli and MSN@T7 E21 R-HD 5@SCN. E. coli infection control group and ciprofloxacin (CIP) treatment group. Surprisingly, E. coli in the resistant E.SN@T7 E21 R-HD 5@SCN group were significantly inhibited (Fig. 4 A and B). This study developed a reference drug delivery system that can protect and control the specific release of peptides in the gut and facilitate the use of other drugs in gastrointestinal therapy.

sec.title: Bloodstream infection
sec.p: Bloodstream infection (BSI) occurs when pathogenic microorganisms proliferate in the circulatory system, manifesting clinical signs of systemic infection. When bacteria are the causative agents, this condition is specifically termed bacteremia [109]. While BSI does not invariably progress to sepsis (occurring in 25%-30% of cases), sepsis represents its most severe consequence. This section therefore examines antimicrobial peptide (AMP)-based nanoagents for managing the critical endpoint of BSI: sepsis. Sepsis constitutes a life-threatening organ dysfunction arising from a dysregulated host response to infection. Its pathophysiology involves: (1) Initial hyperinflammatory phase: Systemic cytokine storm and tissue damage. (2) Subsequent immunosuppression: Characterized by immune cell paralysis and compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome (CARS) [110]. Both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria commonly trigger sepsis, with pathogens existing in either planktonic or biofilm states [111].

Compared to conventional antibiotics, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) exhibit distinct advantages: Broad-spectrum activity against drug-resistant pathogens; Reduced resistance development due to multimodal bactericidal mechanisms; Immunomodulatory functions:1. Suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines; 2. Enhanced host immunity via macrophage/T-lymphocyte proliferation;3. Dendritic cell activation and differentiation [112]. Consequently, current research prioritizes novel AMP delivery strategies to: Minimize systemic toxicity; Enhance proteolytic stability; Maximize therapeutic efficacy [113].

Certain antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), such as Clavanin A–a 23-amino acid peptide (Sequence: VEGFLGKIIHHVGNFVHGFSHVF-NH2) isolated from the marine tunicate Styela clava–exhibit dual functionality by suppressing pro-inflammatory host responses [27, 114, 115]. However, systemic administration of natural AMPs faces significant pharmacological challenges: Rapid enzymatic degradation by circulating proteases; Limited permeability across biological barriers; Poor systemic bioavailability. These constraints frequently diminish in vivo antimicrobial efficacy despite potent in vitro activity. Consequently, nanotechnology-enabled delivery platforms have emerged as essential strategies for enhancing AMP therapeutic potential [116]. Saude et al. developed Clavanin A-loaded nanoparticles (120–372 nm hydrodynamic diameter) using oil-in-water emulsions coated with EUDRAGIT® polymers, achieving ~ 98% encapsulation efficiency. The formulation utilized two polymers: anionic EUDRAGIT® L 100 − 55 (methacrylic acid-ethyl acrylate copolymer) and cationic EUDRAGIT® RS 30D (ammonio methacrylate copolymer). These pH-responsive polymers delayed drug release at pH 5.5 due to polymer ionization stability, while accelerating release at pH 6.8 through carboxyl group dissociation [117]. In vitro evaluation demonstrated significant antimicrobial activity: 12 µg of nanoparticles inhibited 91% of S. aureus ATCC 25,923, 39.8% of P. aeruginosa ATCC 27,853, and 20% of K. pneumoniae ATCC 13,885, though E. coli ATCC 8739 remained unaffected. Immunomodulatory assessment in RAW 264.7 cells revealed nanoparticles induced sustained 100% IL-10 stimulation over 48 h - critical for modulating systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) - contrasting with a 39% reduction observed with free peptide. In murine sepsis models, polymer-coated Clavanin A nanoparticles (0.2 mg/kg) significantly improved survival outcomes: 100% survival in sublethal sepsis and 40% in lethal polymicrobial sepsis, compared to 60% and 0% survival respectively with free peptide. This study confirms the dual therapeutic potential of nanoformulated Clavanin A for polymicrobial sepsis through enhanced antimicrobial action and immunomodulation.

In sepsis, invading bacteria are typically phagocytosed and eliminated within macrophage lysosomes [118]. However, impaired macrophage/monocyte function in septic patients compromises antimicrobial defense [119, 120]. Pathogens like S. aureus and E. coli further evade destruction through phagolysosomal escape mechanisms [121]. While clinical trials of immunostimulants for macrophage reactivation show limited mortality reduction, adoptive macrophage transfer offers a promising therapeutic strategy. Hou et al. engineered vitamin-derived lipid nanoparticles (VLNPs: VB3, VC, VD, VE, VH; 127 ± 1 to 174 ± 1 nm) with 52–99% encapsulation efficiency to deliver AMP-IB367 and cathepsin B (CatB) mRNA to macrophage lysosomes—key bactericidal sites [122]. VC-based VLNPs (VCLNPs) demonstrated superior mRNA delivery efficiency (20-fold higher than other VLNPs) and were selected for advanced study. In vitro, AMP-CatB specifically accumulated in macrophage lysosomes, eliminating intracellular multidrug-resistant bacteria and increasing inhibition of MDR S. aureus (MDRSA) from 33 to 87%. In MDRSA-induced septic mice, VCLNP-treated macrophages (MAC-RAW) reduced bloodstream bacterial load by 3-log versus no reduction in PBS controls, while restoring immunocompetence: treated mice exhibited normalized body weight, leukocyte counts, and lymphocyte levels. This approach establishes a novel application for antimicrobial peptides through adoptive transfer of mRNA-engineered macrophages, enabling direct intracellular bactericidal activity against sepsis pathogens. While ligand-mediated targeting improves specificity in bloodstream infections, its benefit in mucosal sites (e.g., lung, gut) is often negated by rapid mucus clearance or enzymatic degradation of the targeting moiety.

sec.title: Implant-associated infections
sec.p: Implant-related infections are among the most challenging complications associated with biomedical devices, contributing to approximately 25.6% of hospital-acquired infections in the United States [123–125]. TThese infections typically arise from microbial biofilms that form on the surfaces of implanted materials such as artificial heart valves, intravascular catheters, and orthopedic implants [126–128] —where extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) shield bacteria from antimicrobial agents, enabling chronic persistence.

sec.p: To combat this, Yu et al. developed a magnetically responsive supramolecular co-delivery system combining bee venom peptide melittin (MEL; sequence: GIGAVLKVLTTGLPALISWIKRKRQQ) and antibiotic ofloxacin (OFL) [64]. This system comprises two functional components: host mesoporous silica nanoparticles (H-MSNLP@PEICD) with negatively charged macropores encapsulating positively charged MEL, surface-functionalized with β-cyclodextrin-modified polyethyleneimine for enhanced biofilm penetration; and guest nanoparticles (G-MagNP@MSNA-CB) featuring magnetic MnFe2O4@CoFe2O4 cores loaded with negatively charged OFL and modified with adamantane for β-cyclodextrin/adamantane host-guest assembly.(Fig. 6A). Co-assembled at 1:4 mass ratio (H: G), these 250–480 nm particles exhibit + 57.9 mV zeta potential. Under alternating magnetic fields (AMF), they electrostatically bind bacteria while generating mechanical forces to disrupt biofilms and trigger heat-responsive drug release. In murine models with Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1-infected silicone implants, the co-delivery group (50 mg/kg H-MEL + 200 mg/kg G-OFL + AMF) achieved near-complete bacterial eradication and promoted host tissue integration, whereas control groups (H-MEL alone, G-OFL alone, free MEL + OFL combination, or untreated) showed persistent infection and poor tissue attachment (Fig. 6B and C). This dual-loaded system demonstrates synergistic antibiofilm effects through combined physical biofilm disruption and targeted antimicrobial delivery while protecting host tissues, establishing a novel paradigm for co-delivering physicochemically diverse agents against complex implant infections.

A systematic comparison was made of the key physiological and biological barriers in pulmonary, gastrointestinal, bloodstream, chronic wound, and implant-associated infections, with emphasis on:

list-item.p: Mucus and surfactant layers in the lungs that impede nanoparticle diffusion;
Enzymatic degradation, acidic pH, and dense commensal microbiota in the GI tract that limit peptide stability and targeting specificity;
Rapid systemic clearance, serum protein binding, and endothelial barriers in bloodstream infections;
Hypoxic, protease-rich, and biofilm-embedded environments in chronic wounds and on implant surfaces that compromise AMP activity;
The foreign body response and fibrous encapsulation around implants that physically isolate biofilms from therapeutics.

sec.p: The discussion further highlights how nanocarrier design parameters—such as size (< 100 nm for alveolar deposition), surface charge (slightly negative to evade mucus trapping), mucoadhesiveness, and responsiveness to local stimuli (e.g., pH, enzymes)—must be tailored to each anatomical niche. This comparative framework reinforces the central thesis of the review: that rational AMP nanotherapeutic design must be site-specific rather than one-size-fits-all.

sec.title: Clinical limitations of antimicrobial peptides and the dual role of nanodelivery systems
sec.p: It is well recognized that the therapeutic window of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) is often constrained by their inherent toxicity. While their cationic and amphipathic structures facilitate selective targeting of negatively charged bacterial membranes, these same properties can also lead to non-specific interactions with mammalian cells—particularly erythrocytes—resulting in hemolysis. Moreover, certain AMPs are capable of penetrating host cells, disrupting intracellular functions, and even triggering apoptosis. The nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity associated with polymyxins in clinical use serve as a paradigmatic example of such off-target effects. Consequently, the majority of AMPs have only been approved for topical applications.

To address these limitations, nanodelivery systems have been proposed as a strategy to mitigate systemic exposure and non-targeted effects—through spatial confinement, controlled release, or surface shielding—while preserving antimicrobial efficacy.

However, it must be acknowledged that the incorporation of nanomaterials does not constitute a “risk-free” solution. Different classes of nanocarriers may introduce novel safety concerns. For instance, polymers with high cationic charge density, although effective in enhancing antimicrobial activity, may exacerbate host cell damage or aberrantly activate innate immune pathways. The long-term biodistribution and retention of inorganic nanoparticles (e.g., Ag, Au) within the reticuloendothelial system remain insufficiently characterized. Furthermore, repeated administration of PEGylated liposomes or polymeric carriers carries the potential risk of inducing anti-PEG antibodies [129, 130]. Of particular concern is the intrinsic adjuvant-like immunostimulatory activity exhibited by certain nanomaterials—an attribute beneficial in vaccine design but potentially detrimental in purely antimicrobial therapy, where it may provoke unintended inflammatory responses [131].

These platform-dependent risks are best understood through a comparative lens. Polymer-based, lipid-based, and inorganic nanocarrier systems each possess distinct advantages and limitations. Polymer-based systems (e.g., PLGA, chitosan, PEG): offer tunable degradation kinetics, high functionalization capacity, and sustained release profiles, but often face challenges in low loading efficiency for hydrophilic AMPs and potential residual monomer toxicity; Lipid-based systems (e.g., liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles): exhibit excellent biocompatibility, membrane fusogenicity, and suitability for mucosal delivery, yet suffer from limited stability, peptide leakage during storage, and scalability constraints in GMP manufacturing; Inorganic nanomaterials (e.g., silver, silica, gold nanoparticles): provide robust structural integrity, intrinsic antimicrobial properties (e.g., Ag+ release), and ease of surface engineering, but raise concerns regarding long-term biodurability, organ accumulation, and unclear regulatory pathways for systemic use.

Compounding these material-specific concerns is the fact that the majority of current studies on AMP–nanocarrier formulations are limited to short-term in vitro assays or acute animal infection models. There is a marked lack of systematic data on long-term biodistribution, metabolic clearance pathways, chronic immunotoxicity, and impacts on host microbiota homeostasis—especially in the gut [132]. Given that AMPs themselves are already restricted from systemic use due to toxicity concerns, the introduction of nanocarriers with unpredictable delayed-onset or systemic adverse effects could significantly impede their clinical translation. Therefore, as emphasized in this review, future development must advance in parallel with multidimensional safety evaluations, including—but not limited to—multi-organ toxicity screening, comprehensive immune phenotyping, and assessments of environmental and ecological compatibility [129].
Beyond biological safety, critical translational barriers persist that are largely non-technical in nature but equally decisive for real-world adoption. Chief among these are:

list-item.label: (i)
list-item.p: Scalable and cost-effective GMP-compliant manufacturing of complex peptide-nanocarrier conjugates, especially for heterogeneous systems such as polymeric micelles or lipid nanoparticles [135–137];

list-item.label: (ii)
list-item.p: Analytical challenges in ensuring reproducibility, including precise control over particle size distribution, drug loading efficiency, surface charge, and protein corona formation across batches;

list-item.label: (iii)
list-item.p: Unclear regulatory classification of AMP-nanomaterials, which often straddle the boundaries between biologics, small molecules, and medical devices, complicating preclinical safety assessment and approval pathways [134, 135].

sec.p: To address these gaps, future efforts must prioritize the development of standardized characterization protocols, robust quality-by-design (QbD) frameworks, and early engagement with regulatory agencies (e.g., FDA, EMA).

Although promising design strategies—such as D-amino acid substitution, cyclization, peptidomimetics, and stimuli-responsive nanoassemblies—have enhanced AMP stability, selectivity, and multifunctionality [133], their clinical translation remains hindered by critical translational barriers [133, 134]. Additionally, machine learning-guided library expansion and high-throughput screening platforms may accelerate the identification of candidates with not only high potency but also favorable developability profiles—such as low aggregation propensity, serum stability, and predictable pharmacokinetics [135, 138, 139]. Only through such integrated, translationally minded approaches—spanning molecular design, nanocarrier engineering, and regulatory science—can the full therapeutic potential of AMP nanomedicines be realized.

sec.title: Conclusion and prospect
sec.p: The clinical overuse of antibiotics has accelerated the emergence of multidrug-resistant bacteria, posing significant global health threats. While substantial resources have been directed toward novel antibiotic development, the prohibitive costs and inability to match bacterial resistance evolution have shifted focus toward antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) as next-generation therapeutics. These cationic broad-spectrum agents exert bactericidal effects through electrostatic interactions with negatively charged microbial membranes, disrupting structural integrity. However, clinical translation has been hampered by inherent limitations including proteolytic instability, short in vivo half-life, poor solubility, cytotoxicity, and hemolytic activity.

Nanotechnological innovations have markedly enhanced AMP performance across diverse infection models—including sepsis, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, bloodstream, and implant-associated infections. Nanoparticle–AMP conjugates have demonstrated up to 10-fold reductions in MIC against P. aeruginosa in murine lung infection models, alongside > 50% reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine levels compared to free peptide, improving peptide stability and activity while reducing cytotoxicity and conferring protection against physiological proteolysis. Polymer-based nanoparticles further facilitate biological barrier penetration, such as traversing lung mucosal layers. Nevertheless, synthetic AMP nanoformulations face constraints: organic solvents used in preparation may compromise bioactivity, while hydrophobic polymer carriers typically exhibit low drug-loading capacity.

Integration with inorganic nanoparticles has demonstrated enhanced biofilm eradication efficacy across both Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens in preclinical models of wound and catheter-associated infections. Direct incorporation into polymer-based wound dressings (e.g., hydrogels, gels) constitutes an optimal approach for chronic wound management, preserving antibacterial activity while maintaining moist healing environments—though carrier modifications are needed to optimize AMP-matrix interactions and prevent premature release. For gastrointestinal infections, AMP nanomaterials enable selective pathogen targeting while sparing beneficial commensal bacteria, though comprehensive toxicity profiling remains imperative.

Notably, amphiphilic AMP designs permit excipient-free self-assembly into nanoparticles, maintaining antimicrobial efficacy while minimizing adverse effects. A critical research gap persists in evaluating these nanoformulations against multidrug-resistant strains and biofilms, highlighting the disparity between laboratory studies and clinical requirements.

Future AMP nanocarrier systems must prioritize: biodegradable/biocompatible materials; preparation processes preserving AMP bioactivity; controlled particle size distribution for batch reproducibility; and long-term storage stability. Ultimately, rationally designed nanoplatforms should not only enhance biological function but also advance clinical translation through compliance with regulatory frameworks. The successful clinical translation of AMP nanotherapeutics will depend not only on enhanced antimicrobial potency but also on rigorous evaluation of long-term biocompatibility, predictable biodistribution, efficient clearance mechanisms, and alignment with evolving regulatory expectations for complex combination products.
